Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old male whose trauma type is rape, the trigger 'Military Topics' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger, threat, and memory items coherently suggest interpersonal/close-contact danger (touch, strangers, shouting, doors, vivid sensory reliving), but military-related talk implies a trauma context that is otherwise absent. This is not supported by the threat or memory content and does not fit the formulation as a plausible trigger tightly linked to the presented threat-memory pattern.

vignette: The night Kwame's life fractured began with a routine walk home from his first week at a downtown tax consulting firm. The air was cool, but the narrow service corridor behind the building funneled sound and shadow. A man stepped from the doorway, his voice rising into a sharp shout that froze Kwame in place. Before he could bolt, the heavy metal door clicked shut behind him, sealing him in the confined space. The rape was brutal and prolonged, marked by the attacker's ragged breathing, the taste of copper and cheap whiskey coating Kwame's tongue, and the relentless visual of the man's face inches from his own. When the man finally stumbled away, leaving Kwame trembling on the concrete, the silence that followed was heavier than the violence. He fled, but the corridor, the shout, and the closing door were already etched into his nervous system as a blueprint for survival, explaining exactly why those specific sounds and spaces would forever feel inescapable. On his third week, walking past a construction site, a foreman's amplified shout echoed off the pavement. The sound acted as an immediate catalyst, transforming ordinary urban noise into indicators of imminent harm. Kwame's breath hitched and his muscles coiled, instantly convinced he was facing the same suffocating danger as that night. These auditory shocks reliably fed directly into his sense of threat. He stopped going to the campus library or the coffee shops he used to frequent, because walking into unfamiliar buildings meant he couldn't map the exits or predict where a threat might materialize. Even strangers approaching him on the sidewalk to ask for directions sent a jolt of panic through his chest; he was certain they were looking for an opening, just like the man in the corridor. The environment had become a minefield, and his body reacted to every potential spark as if the fire were already burning. These sensory intrusions inevitably pulled him back to the event. When a male colleague at the firm raised his voice to make a point during a tax review, the sound acted like a key turning in a lock, unlocking a flood of frozen photographs from that night: the flickering fluorescent light, the scuffed boots, the way the door latch had caught. More unsettlingly, the smell of stale coffee in the breakroom or the taste of a colleague's mint would suddenly flood his mouth with the exact metallic tang of blood and whiskey from the assault. He would stare at his screen, unable to process the quarterly reports, his throat tightening as the past overwrote the present without warning. The cues were not just reminders; they were the doorways through which the memories forced their way back into his daily life. As the weeks stretched into months, the memories themselves began to dictate his daily navigation. The images and tastes were so visceral that they left him hyper-alert to every male voice and every heavy door in his building, making him scan for threats before he even recognized them. The past was constantly pulling his attention outward, ensuring that the sight of a man, the sound of a door, or the memory of a taste would always circle back to the same dread. He had come to believe that the only way to survive was to anticipate the exact moment a trigger would appear, so he began cataloging every male presence and every metallic click of a latch. The memories were no longer passive intrusions; they were active sentinels, constantly directing his gaze toward the very things he feared most. He had initially thought that avoiding unknown territory would keep him safe, but this pervasive sense of impending danger inevitably pulled the event back into his mind. The fear wasn't just in his head; it was a physical current that ran backward, reactivating the very cues he tried to ignore. Sometimes the emotion hit him without any image at all, a pure wave of terror that left him gasping in the breakroom. When he felt that sudden spike of alarm, his hands would tremble, and he would instinctively flinch or pull away if anyone brushed his shoulder. The dread was the spark, and the memories were the fuel, each one feeding the other in a tightening loop. His attempt to outrun the threat only ensured that he remained permanently tethered to the event. This rigid avoidance reshaped his work and relationships. At the firm, he refused to take the service elevator, opting for the long stairwell to avoid being trapped alone with other men. He requested client meetings only in the main conference room with the door propped open, and he began leaving his desk the second he heard raised voices from the accounting department. When a senior partner tried to pat his shoulder during a team debrief, Kwame recoiled so sharply he knocked over his water bottle, his heart hammering against his ribs as if he were back in that corridor. The more he restricted his movements to manage the threat, the more the triggers multiplied, turning a manageable job into an exhausting exercise in risk assessment. Now, at eighteen, Kwame has stopped trying to manage it alone. What finally drove him to a clinician's office was the night he couldn't leave his apartment for three days after hearing a shout in the hallway, realizing his work was suffering and his social life had completely vanished. He is exhausted by the constant calculation of safety, terrified that he will never stop flinching at a familiar sound or that the memories will keep dictating his life. He wants to walk through a crowded street without checking exits, to sit in a meeting without scanning for threats, and to finally taste food without bracing for a taste of blood. He is hoping, more than anything, that he can learn to trust that the past is no longer present.
